## Simple explanation

A sparse matrix contains mostly zeros. Instead of storing every zero, a
sparse representation stores the nonzero values and where they occur.

## Technical explanation

Sparsity is the fraction of zero entries in a matrix. Formats such as
compressed sparse row (CSR) store nonzeros with index structures; other
formats suit different access patterns. Sparse operations can save storage
and computation when sparsity is high enough and supported by the hardware
and libraries.

## Why it matters in AI engineering

Sparse matrices occur in graph data, one-hot features, recommendation
systems, and pruned neural networks. Choosing a storage format affects
memory, operation speed, and compatibility with downstream libraries.

## How it works

Instead of allocating dense storage, a sparse format records nonzero values
and their positions or row/column boundaries. Algorithms operate on these
entries while avoiding zero multiplications, although indexing and
irregular memory access add overhead.

## Practical example

A user-item interaction matrix may have millions of possible cells but
only a small number of observed ratings. A CSR matrix stores those ratings
without allocating a value for every unobserved pair.

## Common misconceptions

- Sparse data is not automatically faster; small matrices or unsupported
  operations may run better in dense form.
- An unobserved value is not always equivalent to a known zero, especially
  in recommendation and missing-data problems.
